query:
our client, Amani Logistics Limited (a small transport firm), entered into an informal transport and warehousing agreement via WhatsApp with Bora Wholesalers Limited to haul and store Ksh 850,000 worth of imported electronics.

The terms were agreed over a WhatsApp chat thread and confirmed by an M-Pesa deposit receipt. While the goods were stored at Amani Logistics’ leased godown, third-party security guards employed by Shield Security Ltd (an independent security firm hired by Amani) burgled the premises and stole the entire consignment.

Bora Wholesalers was indemnified by its commercial insurer, Apex Insurance Co. Apex Insurance, exercising its rights of subrogation, files a claim against Amani Logistics in the Small Claims Court (SCC Case No. E112/2026) claiming Ksh 850,000 for breach of bailment.

Service of the Statement of Claim was effected on Amani Logistics’ director via WhatsApp. Because Amani’s director was out of the country, he missed the message, leading to an ex-parte default judgment being entered against Amani Logistics. Execution has now commenced via warrants of attachment. Furthermore, Apex Insurance did not attach a Section 106B Certificate of Electronic Evidence for the WhatsApp threads or M-Pesa receipts relied upon in the trial court.

Amani Logistics instructs you to urgently apply to set aside the default judgment, stay execution, and challenge Apex Insurance’s subrogated claim.
